node.title: Re: constant vector (updated x2)
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
Either replace

use constant D50 => [96.42, 100, 82.49];

with

sub D50 () { [96.42, 100, 82.49] }

because this will do the same thing as [doc://constant] (it creates an [doc://perlsub#Constant-Functions|inlineable sub]), but the sub will return a new arrayref every time, or do this:

use Readonly; Readonly::Array my @D50 => (96.42, 100, 82.49); print $D50[0], "\n"; $D50[0]++; __END__ 96.42 Modification of a read-only value attempted at ...

But I've also had some strange problems with [mod://Readonly] (Update: [https://rt.cpan.org/Public/Bug/Display.html?id=64814|link]), so my approach nowadays to constants is simpler: make their names uppercase and assume people know this convention. (But I did need some time to get used to this idea, since I do tend to code defensively.)

Update: Sorry, [doc://B::Deparse] seems to say that I was incorrect and the sub I showed does not seem to get inlined. Will update when I know more. Update 2: So testing seems to show the equivalent code to what [doc://constant] is doing (with the same problem that the array may be modified!) is this:

BEGIN { my $x = [96.42, 100, 82.49]; *D50 = sub () { $x }; }

While other forms, such as simply my $x = [96.42, 100, 82.49]; sub D50 () { $x }, don't get inlined. And I believe the reason sub D50 () { [96.42, 100, 82.49] } doesn't get inlined is exactly what I said above: it constructs a new arrayref on each call, thereby it is not constant. I made this mistake because of the equivalence of use constant FOO => "bar"; and sub FOO () { "bar" }. As [LanX] points out in the reply, my first suggestion will still work, but just not be as fast as an inlined sub. As another possible alternative, note that [doc://constant] also allows list constants:

use constant D50 => (96.42, 100, 82.49);

Which you then have to access like so: (D50)[0]

Update 3: While it's fairly well known that the output of [doc://B::Deparse] can be inaccurate, I think it's still noteworthy that it is misleading in this case in particular.

$ perl -MO=Deparse -e 'use constant X=>[1]; print X->[0]++; print X->[0]++' use constant ('X', [1]); print [1]->[0]++; print [1]->[0]++; $ perl -le 'use constant X=>[1]; print X->[0]++; print X->[0]++' 1 2
